## One sentence. Build three pretraining examples. {#synthesis-pause .syn-slide}

<p class="syn-source"><span>GIVEN · WORD POSITIONS FOR THIS EXERCISE</span>1 the · 2 cat · 3 sat · 4 on · 5 the · 6 mat</p>
<div class="syn-pause-panel"><span class="syn-pause-badge">PAUSE · WORK IN PAIRS · 2 MINUTES</span><h3>Write the model input(s) and the loss targets for each recipe.</h3><p>Mark which positions receive a direct loss. Keep the target separate from the input that predicts it.</p></div>
<div class="syn-rules"><div><b>BERT</b><p>Select positions <strong>2 and 6</strong>; use the <strong>[MASK]</strong> branch for both. Omit [CLS] and [SEP].</p></div><div><b>GPT</b><p>Use <strong>the</strong> as initial context. Score the remaining observed words. No START or EOS in this window.</p></div><div><b>T5</b><p>Remove <strong>cat</strong> and <strong>mat</strong> as separate spans. Include source, decoder input, and decoder target.</p></div></div>
<p class="syn-conventions"><strong>T5 conventions:</strong> S₀/S₁ identify the gaps; S₂ closes the last span. Append EOS to source and target. Shift the decoder input using START.</p>
<p class="s1-source">Fixed teaching choices, not random sampling or literal corruption-rate estimates. Use the same boundary conventions as the preceding GPT and T5 examples. Solution on the following slide.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 4 minutes: introduce the fixed conventions (1), paired work (2), collect
initial answers without displaying the solution (1). This is a synthesis activity,
not a new prediction lesson or loss arithmetic exercise. Students have all the
mechanisms; ask them to construct the training objects precisely.

Read the source positions, emphasizing that the two occurrences of the are distinct.
The corruption choices are supplied, so there is no ambiguity over which tokens
are selected or whether a BERT selected token remains unchanged. We isolate BERT's
MLM part; NSP is outside this token-construction exercise. Its special tokens are
omitted for readability, not forgotten in the real recipe.

GPT follows our new section's no-START finite-window convention, rather than the
old preserved draft's extra start-token example. T5 follows the current paper-style
final-sentinel and explicit EOS convention. START is a decoder input initialization
symbol, not an extra target. No output rows, target counts, or solutions are shown
on this prompt slide, even as fragments. Let students write them before advancing.

Ask groups to check whether any target has accidentally been supplied to its own
prediction. Do not reject T5 source EOS merely because it has no loss of its own;
inputs and scored labels have different roles. Transition: “Compare your constructed
objects with these three worked examples.”
:::

## Same text, three worked constructions {#synthesis-solution .syn-slide}

<p class="syn-source syn-source-compact"><span>UNCHANGED SOURCE</span>the cat sat on the mat</p>
<table class="syn-recipe-table"><thead><tr><th>Recipe</th><th>Model input(s)</th><th>Direct loss targets</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th>BERT<br><small>MLM only</small></th><td>the <b>[MASK]</b> sat on the <b>[MASK]</b></td><td><b>cat</b> at position 2<br><b>mat</b> at position 6<br><small>Other positions: no direct MLM term</small></td></tr><tr><th>GPT</th><td>the cat sat on the</td><td>cat · sat · on · the · mat<br><small>Aligned to the five input positions</small></td></tr><tr><th>T5</th><td><span class="syn-row-label">ENCODER</span>the S₀ sat on the S₁ EOS<br><span class="syn-row-label">DECODER</span>START S₀ cat S₁ mat S₂</td><td>S₀ · cat · S₁ · mat · S₂ · EOS<br><small>Sentinels and EOS are targets too</small></td></tr></tbody></table>
<p class="syn-takeaway">Targets come from the same text; the <strong>supervised positions and available context differ</strong>.</p>
<p class="s1-source">Reuses the preserved three-recipe comparison, updated to this lecture's GPT boundary convention. S₀/S₁/S₂ are sentinel aliases. Constructed examples, not model outputs.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 3 minutes, within the five-minute comparison block. Compare each row with
students' answers. BERT has two selected output positions: cat and mat. The output
positions of the encoder stay aligned with input positions; there is no causal
shift in this MLM construction. The other context states still affect the loss
and can receive gradients even though they have no direct MLM term.

GPT has five predictions, because the first the supplies context and no separate
START token is included. Its row is a sequence of observed inputs processed under
the familiar causal restriction. The target cat belongs to the first input column,
sat to the second, and mat to the last. Do not introduce an extra next word after
mat or count the first the as a target in this specified window.

T5 has a source stream and shifted decoder stream. The target is the ordered
missing spans with sentinel delimiters and EOS. There are six target tokens in
this word-level example, including three sentinels and EOS. The source EOS has
no separate loss term. The final sentinel closes the paper-style target and is
not a third gap. These explicit teaching boundaries need not match every data
pipeline implementation.

Ask students to correct one discrepancy in their own construction. The numbers
of scored targets do not rank model quality. Each objective sees different context
and solves a different prediction problem. Transition: “What does each training
signal act on, and which contextual information is permitted?”
:::

## Compare the supervision and the parameters it trains {#synthesis-comparison .syn-slide}

<div class="syn-family-cards"><div><h3>BERT</h3><span class="syn-label">CONTEXT FOR A TARGET</span><p>Both sides of the <strong>corrupted input</strong></p><span class="syn-label">PARAMETERS LEARNED</span><p>Embeddings, encoder, and pretraining heads</p><span class="syn-family-foot">Original recipe also included NSP.</span></div><div><h3>GPT</h3><span class="syn-label">CONTEXT FOR A TARGET</span><p>The observed <strong>prefix</strong></p><span class="syn-label">PARAMETERS LEARNED</span><p>Embeddings, causal decoder, and vocabulary head</p><span class="syn-family-foot">No task labels needed for corpus LM training.</span></div><div><h3>T5</h3><span class="syn-label">CONTEXT FOR A TARGET</span><p>The <strong>corrupted source</strong> and earlier target tokens</p><span class="syn-label">PARAMETERS LEARNED</span><p>Embeddings, encoder, decoder, and vocabulary head</p><span class="syn-family-foot">Decoder loss also trains the encoder.</span></div></div>
<p class="syn-takeaway">Architecture controls information access. The objective chooses the supervision. <strong>Pretraining changes weights.</strong></p>
<p class="syn-caption">More targets—or a smaller loss under a different objective—does not establish a better pretrained model.</p>
<p class="s1-source">Synthesis of the preceding BERT, GPT, and T5 sections. Representative recipes, not exclusive capabilities. Shared/tied embeddings remain shared parameters.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 2 minutes, completing the five-minute comparison block. This is a recall
check, not a repeat of the attention diagrams. Ask one group to name the context
for a BERT target, another for GPT, another for T5. A BERT MASK token has access
to both sides of the supplied corrupted input, not the original removed word.
T5 sees all of its corrupted source through encoder memory and only the previous
targets on the decoder side. Future output targets are never provided to their
own predictions in the causal branches.

Then ask what is learned. During pretraining, both T5 stacks learn even though
its direct target loss is on the decoder. BERT's context-only input states can
also receive gradients through selected outputs. The original NSP head belongs
to original BERT's pretraining recipe; it is not a downstream sentiment head.
Some pretraining heads will be replaced or adapted later, while the learned
backbone supplies initialization for a new task.

Keep architecture, objective, and training stage distinct. A decoder can be
adapted for classification; an encoder–decoder can output a class label. These
are not exclusive task lists. Losses with different targets, tokenizations,
and conditioning are not a controlled downstream benchmark. Transition: “Which
objects survive as a reusable model after this training process?”
:::

## We reuse weights. We compute new representations. {#synthesis-weights .syn-slide}

```{=html}
<svg class="syn-weights-diagram" viewBox="0 0 1320 370" role="img" aria-label="A saved checkpoint contains learned weights. Supplying a new sentence to those weights computes new contextual states. Those states are outputs for that input, while the saved parameters can be reused again.">
<defs><marker id="sw-arrow" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10Z" fill="#0f7881"/></marker></defs>
<g font-family="sans-serif" fill="#17364a" text-anchor="middle"><rect x="35" y="140" width="365" height="145" rx="12" fill="#17364a"/><text x="217" y="192" font-size="28" fill="white" font-weight="bold">SAVED CHECKPOINT θ*</text><text x="217" y="243" font-size="27" fill="white">learned parameter arrays</text>
<rect x="485" y="20" width="515" height="75" rx="12" fill="#f0e6d4"/><text x="742" y="68" font-size="32">“I loved this film.”</text><path d="M742 105V158" stroke="#0f7881" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#sw-arrow)"/>
<path d="M410 210H555" stroke="#0f7881" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#sw-arrow)"/><rect x="570" y="170" width="340" height="115" rx="12" fill="#dfece6"/><text x="740" y="218" font-size="29">Forward computation</text><text x="740" y="257" font-size="25">uses the saved weights</text>
<path d="M920 225H1025" stroke="#0f7881" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#sw-arrow)"/><rect x="1040" y="170" width="250" height="115" rx="12" fill="#dde8f0"/><text x="1165" y="217" font-size="32">h₁, h₂, …</text><text x="1165" y="259" font-size="24">contextual states</text>
<text x="217" y="345" font-size="26">Reusable across inputs</text><text x="1040" y="345" font-size="26">Computed for this input</text></g></svg>
```

<div class="syn-target-sources"><div><span class="syn-label">PRETRAINING TARGET</span><strong>cat</strong><p>Retained from the observed corpus text.</p></div><div><span class="syn-label">DOWNSTREAM TASK LABEL</span><strong>positive</strong><p>A sentiment annotation for this review.</p></div></div>
<p class="syn-takeaway">The checkpoint provides a learned starting point. A new task still needs a defined output and appropriate supervision or use strategy.</p>
<p class="s1-source">Conceptual distinction between parameters, activations, and labels. The review label is authored; no model prediction is shown. Keep the matching tokenizer and configuration with the weights.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 3 minutes. Students often conflate weights, contextual vectors, and targets.
Trace the saved parameter arrays into the computation; the same arrays can process
another sentence and produce different contextual states. At ordinary inference,
the changed input changes the activations, not the stored weights. Further training
can of course update those weights; Session 2 will distinguish the choices.

The saved checkpoint is not a list of all possible contextual vectors or all task
labels. It contains parameter arrays, and its matching tokenizer/configuration
are needed to use it correctly. Learned weights can memorize some training text;
this distinction is not a claim that memorization is impossible.

Below the diagram, cat and positive are different kinds of target. The former
came from the observed corpus under our corruption rule. The latter comes from
a sentiment annotation for I loved this film. Neither is a hidden-state vector.
Nor should positive be taken as the output of the displayed forward computation:
we have not yet defined the task-specific prediction mapping on this slide.

The diagram uses generic contextual states to illustrate the parameter/output
distinction; it does not prescribe the same readout for all three architectures.
Pretraining alone does not guarantee success on the new task. Prompted use may
keep weights fixed, while supervised adaptation may change them; reserve those
mechanisms for Session 2. Transition: “What must connect these pretrained states
to the new sentiment decision?”
:::

<p class="syn-final-question">We trained a word predictor.<br>How can it become a sentiment classifier?</p>
<p class="syn-ending-caption">Next session: define the task output, decide which weights change, and evaluate on new examples.</p>

::: {.notes}
TIME: 3 minutes. This is the actual visual ending of Session 1. The three-model
comparison is complete; do not add Session 2's contents slide or teach its head
or update equations before review. Keep the intellectual gap in the middle box.

Trace the upper path: corpus pretraining supplied learned parameters. Trace the
lower path: a new task supplies labeled examples, with positive as an annotation
for this review. These ingredients meet at adaptation, whose mechanism remains
open. The diagram does not claim that every adaptation strategy must update all
weights, or that labels are needed for every possible form of pretrained-model
use. It previews our next concrete supervised sentiment example.

Ask students to suggest what must be specified: an output space, a connection
from the learned representation to that output, and a learning/use procedure.
Collect suggestions without giving the full solution. Save the distinctions
between a new head, frozen features, full fine-tuning, and prompting for Session 2.
The rightmost words name the allowed labels, not measured predictions. Motion
represents dependency flow, not a running training algorithm.

Conclude with the exact displayed question. Students should leave with the causal
story: text supplies targets; an objective trains parameters; those parameters
are reusable, but a new task requires a defined way to use them. Stop here.
:::
